html:
The Kingdom of Sicily was a kingdom in southern Italy, founded by the Normans in 1130. At first it held both the island of Sicily and the mainland south, and after 1282 the name was used by two separate kingdoms. The map follows that: in 1279 and 1300 the label sits on the mainland, in 1400 on both, and from 1530 to 1715 on the island alone.

Before the Normans, Sicily had been an Arab emirate. Norman knights took the island between 1061 and 1091, and Roger II was crowned king at Palermo in 1130. His court mixed Latin, Greek and Arab learning; the geographer al-Idrisi made his great map for him. The emperor Frederick II grew up in Palermo and ruled from there.

In 1266 the pope gave the kingdom to Charles of Anjou. Sicilians rose against his French officials in the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 and called in the king of Aragon. From then on the island belonged to Aragon and later Spain, while the mainland stayed with the Angevins and became known as the Kingdom of Naples. Both called themselves the Kingdom of Sicily.

Spanish viceroys ruled the island for centuries; it exported grain, and after the earthquake of 1693 its south-eastern towns were rebuilt in Baroque style. It passed to Savoy in 1713, to Austria in 1720 and to a Spanish Bourbon prince in 1734. In 1816 the island and Naples were merged as the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.
